content.title: Answers for Weaknesses
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments. 

Q1
FedMAE has the lowest GFLOPs due to the short length and 75% mask ratio, so the computing power requirements of FedMAE will not increase higher than CNNs with the increase in image size.

Q2
Current FSSL methods are not very good at learning large-scale image data in the scenario of federated learning. We apply a small transformer to solve this problem well, which has a huge improvement (30% to 50%) over state-of-the-art baselines.

Q3
The experiment proves the rationality of FedMAE. Although there is no theoretical support at present, we believe that there will be in the future.

Q4
We also compared the Params and GFLOPs of our downstream model in Table 2.  Compared to other methods, the computation resources required for FedMAE are acceptable.

Q5 & Q6 &Q7
We will analyze the effect of the added classifier in the downstream training. 
We will put more visualization results of the one-block pre-training model.
We will elaborate more details of multi-round communication in section 3.

content.title: Answers for some Comments
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments.

Q1
Process 2 explains how FedMAE is trained in FL. We only rely on the server to transfer model weight.

Q2 
When an image with all zero pixels enters our system, the output of the encoder is a zero tensor, i.e., h(0) = 0. Consequently, the output of the decoder is also a reconstruction image with all zero pixels, i.e., g(0) = 0. Therefore, there exists a zero reference point for discussing the encoder and decoder operators. Then, expand the nonlinear vector function h(x) into a Taylor series at 0, which can approximately be seen as a linear equivalent mapping. The details are shown in 4.2.
We model an approximate mapping for FedMAE and give an approximate analytical solution to optimal reconstruction, which only depends on the data. A good pre-training model can make the better performance of the downstream model.

Q3
The fed-avg method does not improve our model performance due to the small learning rate in the transformer. Not using fed-avg also allows our entire system to be trained fully asynchronously without aggregation in the server.
We only use partially labeled data for downstream tasks without using any specific semi-supervised learning algorithm.

content.title: Answers for Weaknesses
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments. We will check each section in detail and fix the typos and writing issues. The major comments can be divided into two aspects. 

For questions of Method exposition
- If the downstream task only needs five blocks, then only five one-block MAEs will be trained in FL and the total pre-training models in FL are five. 
- We use rounds to be fair with other methods’ settings. The experiment setting is a common setting in the FSSL scenario. All the methods use 200 rounds for training in our paper. 
- The average operation is not effective. Not using fed-avg also allows our entire system to be trained fully asynchronously without aggregation in the server. 
- We also use Imagenet as our pretraining dataset in some experiments.

For questions of Theoretical analysis

In this paper, we theoretically analyze the equivalence between missing information and feature interference in a distributed learning scenario and give an analytic form of a feasible solution to the problem that depends only on the data, thus proving that the problem is solvable. However, computing with analytic solutions requires a lot of memory and arithmetic power, which is not feasible in practice, so we designed a solver based on MAE with FedMAE design. Experimentally, the solving performance of our method is proved to be better than that of FSSL. Proposition 1, Corollary 1, Theorem 1, and Theorem 2 recursively give the analytic form of optimal reconstruction for a single client and multiple clients in a distributed non-complete information scenario, which is the basis for the subsequent design of the solver, since the existence of a solution is a prerequisite for solvability. For space reasons, easy-to-solve derivations are omitted from the text. 

Since the mapping h is designed, smoothness is guaranteed. Setting WgWh = W, one obtains the reformulation of the problem (5). The derivation of Theorems 1 and 2 reveals that a theoretical analytic solution can be obtained for the equivalent quadratic form, thus proving that the reformulation can be accomplished by a local approximate linear mapping, and the work of this paper is to solve this mapping by the method we have devised. Due to space limitations, some proof derivations are not given, but we will further refine the theoretical description.

Current FSSL methods are not very good at learning large-scale image data in the scenario of federated learning. We first apply a small transformer to solve this problem well, which has a huge improvement (30% to 50%) over state-of-the-art baselines.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

S1: To conduct large scale pretraining in FL setting is an important task;

Weakness:

1). The writing of the paper is very hard to follow. Basically, it is not self-contained. For example, MAE is frequently used in the draft. However, in the method section, there is no formal definition of what MAE is. Meanwhile, many math notations are not defined before use. For example, m is used in the first paragraph in 4.1.2, but was defined its meaning in the next paragraph. Why use the term “source dataset” and “target dataset” in the 4.1.1? Does the paper is for domain adaptation?

2). It is suggested to provide detailed algorithm pseudo-code in the appendix to make it easier to read. 

3). The novelty of the draft is limited. Basically, it is only trying to adopt current ViT pretraining on images in the setting of federated learning. The contribution to federated learning is very limited. The is no challenges to do so. 

4). There are too many typos and grammar errors, indicating the low quality of the draft. For example,
Page 5: “becomes into”==>”becomes”
Page 4: “with lables”==>”with labels”
Page 14: “This increase trend”==>”This increasing trend”

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper investigates the problem of training a vision model with self-supervised learning (SSL) in a federated setting, where clients have little computing power and zero labelled data (cross-device).

The main contribution of the authors is to introduce a method called FedMAE: the idea consists in training single ViT blocks on clients, which is an autoencoder trained to infer masked parts of the image. Crucially, these blocks are trained independently, without averaging. The resulting encoder blocks are then stacked into a large network that can be finetuned on other downstream tasks where labelled data is available.

Experiments in the main paper and in the appendix perform a simulation of FL on mini-Imagenet (either with an IID split or with a synthetic heterogeneity induced by labels), with downstream tasks relying on CIFAR10/100, ROAD SIGN, and Mini-INAT. These experiments tend to demonstrate an improvement of the performance over previously introduced federated SSL approaches.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths

1. The idea is simple and I genuinly think it's a good idea to train single blocks locally and re-combine them for later use

# Weaknesses

2. The paper lacks clarity in many aspects (incl. exposition of the method, theoretical analysis - see detailed clarity comments below). I think major changes are needed to address it.
3. The theoretical analysis does not bring evidence of the advantage of the proposed method, contrary to the claims of the authors (Last sentence of conclusion, "Theoretical analysis (...) show that our FedMAE achieves a considerable boost compare to previous FSSL methods").
    - The corresponding section is not well written (cf 2. and detailed comments below);
    - results are either trivial (Prop. 1, Corollary 1, Theorem 1, Theorem 2), or vague and unproven (Prop 2) or simply unproven (Prop 3) (cf detailed comments below).
    - In its current form (almost 1/3 of the main paper), I don't think it brings anything to the rest of the paper.
4. The method introduced by the authors has a major conceptual challenge: the number of independent MAE blocks grows with the number of clients taking part in FedMAE. This challenge is not ignored by the authors.
5. The experimental section could be improved:
    - Unless mistaken, the authors do not compare to the baseline consisting in training 1 block / client, but with averaging. It is stated in Sec 3.3, step 2, that the average operation is "not necessary (or effective)": it would be better to have a proof of this lack of effectiveness
    - Federated training is only performed on synthetic heterogeneity (dirichlet sampling of mini-imagenet). This is regrettable, especially as the authors use Mini-INAT which has a natural geographical split.
    - (minor) No error bars are provided
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
# Clarity

The paper is not clear and writing could be significantly improved:

- Method exposition:
  - How the method handles the large number of independent blocks (growing with the number of clients) is unclear to me.
  - The paper seems to contradict itself on this question. In the caption of Figure 2, it is stated that (I emphasize)
>Pre-training models in FL can be trained on different clients asynchronously **without average aggregation.**
  
    This is also the meaning I get from Section 3.3, step 2. Therefore, one could imagine that the notion of rounds is meaningless. However, in Sec 5.2, $ setup, details on training rounds for the method are provided.
    > The number of training rounds is set to 200, the number of local epochs is set to 10, the total number of local clients is set to 100, and the participation ratio is set to 0.05
    These details are repeated in App 1.2, indicating that they are specific to the FedMAE method and not to baseline approaches (introduced later). With 100 clients and praticipation ratio of 5 / rounds, one should have touched all clients in 20 rounds. How do the authors explain the number 200?
  - Further, the total number of blocks used in the final ViT seems to be 4 or 5, witness Table 8 and the model sizes in Table 2 (Downstream size /Pretrained size ~ 4). How is it compatible with a choice of 100 clients? If only 4 blocks are used, how are they chosen?
- Theoretical analysis (Sec 4)
  - There are redundancies between the different parts: essentially, Sec 4.1.1 and the beginning of Sec 4.2 contain the same content; further, parts of Sec 4.1.2 is already contained in Sec 4.1.2
  - What does "uniform dimensional encoding" (Sec 4.1.1) mean?
  - Prop 1 is not precise enough in its current wording and essentially trivial: it says that the encoder $h$ can be approximated by a Taylor expansion of order 1 around 0, which is a linear map if its value at 0 is 0. This is only valid if $h$ is smooth, which is not stated as an assumption.
  - The reformulation of problem (5) from a non-convex linear autoencoder $\hat{x} = W_g W_h \tilde{x} $ into a convex one $\hat{x} = W \tilde{x}$ is unjustified and non-trivial
  - Theorems 1 and 2 basically state solutions to quadratic problems, whose solutions are well-known. Further, Eq (7) defines $W_k^* = W^*_{gk} W^*_{hk}$ without defining $W^*_{gk}$ or $W^*_{hk}$
  - Proposition 2 is not precise: "when random sampling is used to corrupt the data $X$", this random sampling is not defined. Further, this proposition is not proven
  - Proposition 3 is not proven

# Quality

- The theoretical analysis does not bring anything to the rest of the paper:
  - in its setup, it is not precise enough: it does not formalize the masking used in the rest of the paper, so it would be hard for it to capture any meaningful result
  - it relies on linear approximations, but deep neural networks are highly non-linear. Although several well-known works have used deep linear maps to understand non-convex optimization behaviour, this section further dismisses this non-convexity with Eq (6) and (7);
  - the end results which might be related to the rest of the paper (Prop 2) are not stated clearly enough and, most importantly, not proven.
- The experiments could be improved (cf above)
  - there is no experimental proof that averaging single MAE blocks is detrimental to performance
  - Only synthetic heterogeneity is used on Mini-Imagenet, which is not realistic
  - No error bars are provided for results: in the supplementary material, the number of independent repetitions used for the experiments is not stated

# Novelty

I think the idea is novel

# Reproducibility

Given the lack of clarity, I would have trouble reproducing the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper seems to introduce an interesting idea, which seems to be working experimentally, but fails to convey it clearly. Further, the paper contains a theoretical analysis encompassing almost 1/3 of the paper which does not bring much to the rest of the paper. I would advise the authors to remove this section, which would give space to better explain the proposed method as well as add experiments. As this entails major changes, I don't think the paper can be accepted to this conference.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a federated self-supervised learning method named Masked AutoEncoder (FedMAE). The Masked AutoEncoder is used in FedMAE to make use of the unlabeled data in the clients. However, due to the limitation of lightweight client devices, FedMAE pre-trains a one-block MAE instead of a normal MAE in each client. In order to aggregate the knowledge from the clients, FedMAE cascades the collected pre-trained one-block MAEs on the server and builds a multi-block ViT backbone for downstream tasks. Experimental results for downstream classification tasks on several datasets show competitive performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The problem setting of this paper is practical. An efficient self-supervised learning method is needed in practical scenarios.  
2. This paper is clearly written and easy to read, benefitting from the lucid framework diagram and a concise introduction to the method.

Weaknesses:
1. The feasibility of using one-block autoencoders on light-weight client devices needs to be proved. Although in the results of table 2, FedMAE has the lowest GFLOPs compared with other methods, with the increase in image size, the computing power requirements of transformers are much higher than that of CNNs with the same number of parameters. 
2. The novelty of the paper (the server collects the client-side MAEs to cascade an aggregated MAE) is limited.
3. Although the input and output of the one-block transformer have the same dimension, the input features are low-level while the output features are high-level. Simply cascading the transformers on the server to form the downstream model may be unreasonable. 
4. For the experimental results in Table 1, FedMAE shows good performance compared to other methods. But the model architectures used in these compared methods for downstream training are different. The downstream model of FedMAE is a transformer with a great depth due to the cascading of client transformers. This comparison seems unfair. 
5. In the downstream tasks’ evaluation, the results of fine-tuning the added classifier are needed to further prove the performance of FedMAE.
6. Some visualization results about the reconstruction in the clients with a one-block autoencoder may help to validate the performance of FedMAE. Whether a simple transformer is sufficient for the reconstruction based on the masked image.
7. In Figure 2, there exist arrows pointing from the server to the clients, but in Section 3.3 there is no explanation to the multi-round communication.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper is easy to follow, but some details are missing or unclear. 
- The novelty of the paper is limited.
- The practical feasibility of this method is still questionable.
- The code is provided and the results may be reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: The problem setting of this paper is practical and the proposed approach to model aggregation is different (but not novel) from existing methods. The proposed approach of cascading clients’ transformers for downstream tasks is somewhat unreasonable. Although this paper makes some efforts to reduce the computing power requirements for the clients, the practical feasibility of this method is still questionable.

content.title: FedMAE: Federated Self-Supervised Learning with One-Block Masked Auto-Encoder
content.abstract: Latest federated learning (FL) methods started to focus on how to use unlabeled data in clients for training due to users' privacy concerns, high labeling costs, or lack of expertise. However, current Federated Semi-Supervised/Self-Supervised Learning (FSSL) approaches fail to learn large-scale images because of the limited computing resources of local clients. In this paper, we introduce a new framework FedMAE, which stands for Federated Masked AutoEncoder, to address the problem of how to utilize unlabeled large-scale images for FL. Specifically, FedMAE can pre-train one-block Masked AutoEncoder (MAE) using large images in lightweight client devices, and then cascades multiple pre-trained one-block MAEs in the server to build a multi-block ViT backbone for downstream tasks. Theoretical analysis and experimental results on image reconstruction and classification show that our FedMAE achieves superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art FSSL methods.
